kurz: Why the size premium is the weakest of the classic premiums, which reasons for second-line shares remain nonetheless and what the bid-ask spread costs there.

bloecke.md:
Second-line shares form a size segment of the stock market, not a separate asset class. In Germany, this segment comprises the shares below the 40 DAX constituents, that is, the 50 companies in the MDAX, the 70 in the SDAX, and Scale, a segment of the open market (Freiverkehr) in which smaller growth companies with reduced post-listing obligations have been listed since 2017. Internationally, MSCI defines the boundary by a calculation rule. The standard indices cover around 85% of the free-float market capitalisation of a market, the small-cap index the next 14% or so. An MSCI World Small Cap therefore contains several thousand constituents and still covers only a small part of global stock market value.

Where the boundary lies is a matter of convention. An SDAX company with a market capitalisation of €800 million counts as a second-line share in German usage and would be close to the micro-cap range in the US. When making statements about small caps, it must therefore be clear which definition is meant, because the return figures depend directly on it.

## Findings on the size premium

In 1981, Rolf Banz showed that small US shares had achieved higher returns over decades than their market beta explained. In 1993, Fama and French turned this into the SMB factor (*Small minus Big*). Over the entire period from July 1926 to July 2026, SMB returns a geometric average of 1.42% a year (arithmetic: 1.99%).

The size premium is the only one of the classic premiums that is not statistically established over a hundred years. Its t-statistic is 1.82. That is enough for the 10% level (threshold 1.645), but not for the usual 5% level (threshold 1.96). Market (4.54), momentum (4.55) and value (3.46) are well above both thresholds. For later periods, the values are even weaker. Since January 1994, SMB has been at -0.29% p.a., since 1981 at -0.21% and from January 2021 to July 2026 at -5.08%. The largest decline of the factor was 54.9%, from the peak in July 1983 to the trough in March 1999. The 1983 peak had still not been regained by July 2026.

The premium was negative in 35% of all rolling ten-year periods since 1926, and in 19.5% of the twenty-year periods. From 1964 to 2025, exactly half of the calendar years were positive, that is, as many as would be expected from pure chance.

bloecke.unter: Long-short factor SMB of the three-factor model, June 1963 = 1, year-end values, 2026 as of July; the monthly peak of July 1983 (3.20) was not regained, and for four decades there was no premium.

bloecke.titel: Size premium by decade (US, geometric p.a.)
bloecke.unter: The premium was negative in six of eleven decades, including the two decades after the 1981 publication.

bloecke.md: The size of a company is a characteristic of its share. No return premium comes with it, not even for investors who deliberately hold second-line shares. Any justification for the segment must therefore do without the sentence “small caps deliver better returns in the long run”.

## Implementability of the premium

Two studies explain why the measured premium could hardly be achieved in practice. Hou, Xue and Zhang recalculated 447 published anomalies. At a threshold of t = 1.96, 64% of them are not significant; at t = 3.0, the figure is 85%. The main reason is methodological, because the original studies weighted the shares equally instead of by market value and included microcaps, that is, shares in which hardly any order can be executed. An equally weighted portfolio of a thousand of the very smallest shares can be calculated in a database, but it cannot be put into practice in a real portfolio.

Chen and Velikov recalculated 204 long-short anomalies, taking into account bid-ask spreads, the decline in returns after publication and modern trading technology. They arrived at an average of four basis points a month, around 0.5% a year. McLean and Pontiff also show that anomaly portfolios made up of illiquid shares with high firm-specific risk achieve higher returns, that is, where arbitrage is expensive. This is also the area in which the size premium was measured.

This overlap is no accident, because the measured premium was to a large extent compensation for illiquidity. Investors who want to capture it have to bear the illiquidity themselves and pay for it with every trade.

## Cost of the bid-ask spread

For DAX shares, the [[Bid-ask spread|bid-ask spread]] on Xetra is in the range of hundredths of a per cent. For thinly traded second-line shares, it varies greatly depending on the share, trading venue and time of day, from a tenth of a per cent to several per cent. It widens precisely when many investors want to sell at the same time. Over a complete round trip of purchase and sale, you pay it once in full, half when buying above the mid price and half when selling below it. What determines the costs is therefore the product of spread and turnover, not the spread alone.

bloecke.titel: Cost of the spread (illustrative calculation, €5,000 position, excluding order fees)

bloecke.md:
Assume a second-line share with a market capitalisation of €120 million, a free float of 40% and an average Xetra turnover of €150,000 a day.

A position of €15,000 then corresponds to 10% of the turnover of an entire trading day. An order for the whole position at once moves the price. Realistically, the exit takes several days with partial executions. After a profit warning, turnover not infrequently falls to a fraction while the spread multiplies. The figures are assumed, but the order of magnitude is commonplace in the German second-line segment.

## Analyst coverage and dispersion

Sharpe's arithmetic also applies to second-line shares. Before costs, the average active return equals the passive return; after costs, it is below it. This is an arithmetical identity and not an empirical finding. It says nothing, however, about the dispersion of results, and this is greater when fewer market participants follow a company. A DAX group is followed by dozens of analysts. For an SDAX or Scale company, there are often one to three, and sometimes only a study commissioned and paid for by the company itself. The MiFID II requirement to pay for research separately has further reduced the coverage of small European companies since 2018. With the 2024 Listing Act package, the EU has relaxed the strict separation again.

This effect can be seen in fund data, but it is considerably smaller than is often assumed.

bloecke.titel: Share of active US funds that beat their passive counterpart over 10 years
bloecke.unter: Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer, as of 30 June 2025; for US small caps, the success rate is three times as high as for US large caps, yet it is still only 18%.

bloecke.md: The figure speaks both for and against active management of second-line shares. In relative terms, the rate is three times as good as in the US large-cap segment, but in absolute terms four out of five funds fail over ten years, even though they are run by professionals with data terminals, access to management and their full working time. On top of this come the costs. Actively managed equity UCITS in the EU had ongoing charges of 1.50% on a ten-year average, traditional index funds 0.53% and ETFs 0.31% (ESMA, period 2012-2021). Funds for second-line shares tend to be at the upper end of this range, because the analysis is more laborious and the capacity smaller. A lead of one percentage point from better analysis is used up before it reaches the portfolio.

- Under Section 33 WpHG (Securities Trading Act), a notification is required when a share of voting rights exceeds or falls below the thresholds of 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 50 or 75%. These **voting rights notifications** are published and, in thinly traded shares, show who is taking up a position.
- For **managers' transactions**, Article 19 MAR (Market Abuse Regulation) imposes a notification requirement within three business days as soon as the total volume in the calendar year reaches €50,000. In Germany, this threshold has applied since 1 January 2026; the EU base value is €20,000. If several board members buy, that is a signal, but not a guarantee.
- At annual general meetings and capital markets days of second-line companies, the management board and supervisory board often answer questions from private shareholders directly. At large corporations, this kind of access practically does not exist.

The first risk concerns execution. In a thin order book, a market order is executed at the prices of the few opposing orders, so the other side determines the price. A stop-loss becomes a market order when it is triggered. In thinly traded shares, even a single small sale can trigger it, and the execution can be far below the stop level. In direct trading outside Xetra hours, you trade with a market maker who prices in their own risk.

The second risk lies in the shareholder structure. A major shareholder with 95% can squeeze out the minority in return for cash compensation under Section 327a AktG (Stock Corporation Act). A domination and profit transfer agreement (Beherrschungs- und Gewinnabführungsvertrag) under Section 291 AktG replaces the prospect of price gains with a fixed compensation payment (Section 304 AktG) and an exit compensation offer (Section 305 AktG). Since 2015, a delisting has required a purchase offer under Section 39(2) and (3) BörsG (Stock Exchange Act). Its price is based on the weighted six-month average price and not on intrinsic value. An investment based on undervaluation can fail because of this.

## Taxation of individual shares and ETFs

Individual second-line shares are treated like all shares for tax purposes. Capital gains are subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375%, and church tax where applicable. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG).

For a concentrated second-line strategy, Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG is particularly important. Under this provision, losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares, that is, neither against dividends nor against interest or ETF gains. An investor who makes a loss on an individual share and otherwise only has gains from funds must carry the loss forward until a gain from a share sale arises again. The separate offsetting limit of €20,000 for derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) and worthless securities was abolished by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz). The separate share loss pot still exists, however.

For a small-cap ETF, on the other hand, the Investment Tax Act (InvStG) applies. For equity funds held as private assets, it provides for a partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% under Section 20(1) InvStG and, for accumulating funds, the annual advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG. Losses from fund units go into the general loss pot. Compared with the individual share, this is a structural advantage that does not appear in any return table.

Two routes remain. The first is to add the segment through a broad, low-cost small-cap index. The justification for this is that a world portfolio without the bottom 14% of market capitalisation is incomplete, and it does not assume a premium, because none has been measurable for thirty years. The second route is selecting individual shares in an area that you know thoroughly, with few positions, limit orders, a long holding period and a willingness to be unable to trade at all if in doubt.

The middle way is expensive: a dozen small shares that are regularly reshuffled in the expectation of a size bonus. There, the spread, fees and loss offsetting restricted to shares add up to a shortfall that the selection first has to make up.

mitnehmen: The size premium is the weakest of the classic premiums, with 1.42% p.a. over a hundred years at t = 1.82 and negative values since 1994.
The largest cost item for second-line shares is the bid-ask spread times turnover; the TER matters less.
Low analyst coverage increases the dispersion of results but not the expected value, and even in the small-cap segment around four out of five active managers fail over ten years.

A thin market is an execution risk, against which limit orders instead of market orders help, and a structural risk, because an anchor shareholder with at least 95% can squeeze out the minority under Section 327a AktG.
Losses on shares can only be offset against gains on shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG), which is why an ETF is more robust for tax purposes than a portfolio of individual shares.

begriffe.text: Long-short return series of small minus large shares according to Fama/French. From 1926 to 2026, it returned around 1.4% p.a., which is not statistically significant, and it has been negative since 1994.

The freely tradable portion of a company's shares. For second-line shares, it is often below 50% because families, founders or anchor investors hold the rest. The free float determines tradability and index weight.
Difference between the highest bid and the lowest offer. It is paid once in full over a complete buy-and-sell cycle.
State of low order book depth. Even small orders move the price, spreads widen in periods of stress, and positions can only be unwound over several days.
Exclusion of the minority shareholders in return for cash compensation by a major shareholder holding at least 95% of the shares (Section 327a AktG).
